question: On respiratory examination, which combination of findings is MOST consistent with severe emphysema (the 'pink puffer' phenotype of COPD)?

answers.text: Barrel chest, hyper-resonant percussion, reduced breath sounds bilaterally, and use of accessory muscles

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Emphysema causes hyperinflation (barrel chest, hyper-resonance, low diaphragm) with air trapping reducing breath sounds; accessory muscle use reflects increased work of breathing.

answers.text: Central cyanosis, pitting oedema, and coarse crackles at both bases

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. These features — cyanosis, oedema, and crackles — are more characteristic of the 'blue bloater' (chronic bronchitis with cor pulmonale), not the emphysematous phenotype.

answers.text: Bilateral wheeze loudest on expiration, normal percussion note, and normal chest expansion

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Bilateral expiratory wheeze with normal percussion is a typical presentation of asthma. Emphysema produces a hyper-resonant note with markedly reduced breath sounds.

answers.text: Fine end-inspiratory crackles, clubbing, and reduced chest expansion symmetrically

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Fine inspiratory crackles and clubbing suggest fibrosing alveolitis (interstitial lung disease), not obstructive airways disease.

overallFeedback.feedback: In emphysema, hyperinflation gives barrel chest and hyper-resonance; air trapping reduces breath sounds; accessory muscle recruitment reflects increased work of breathing.
Well done. Barrel chest + hyper-resonance + quiet breath sounds + accessory muscle use = emphysematous COPD.
